title: Approximating a binomial
objectives: Approximate binomial probabilities with a normal curve and a continuity correction
Place the half-unit correction on the correct side of the event
Choose the Poisson instead when $p$ is near 0 or 1

screens.title: A bell over the bars
screens.prose: The bars are $X \sim \text{Bin}(30, p)$. The dashed curve is a normal with the same mean $np$ and variance $np(1-p)$. Slide $p$ and watch the fit.
screens.question: Slide $p$ down to 0.05. How does the curve fit the bars now?

options.text: Poorly: the bars pile up against 0 and lean right

options.why: Compare the two ends. At 0.05 the curve spills below 0, where the bars cannot go.

options.text: Better, because the bars are taller
options.why: Taller bars mean the chance is squeezed into a few values near 0. The bell cannot squeeze against a wall.

hints.text: Compare the picture at $p = 0.5$ with the picture at $p = 0.05$.
Look at the left edge: where does the curve go that the bars cannot?

feedback.correct: Near $p = 0$ the bars are lopsided and the bell is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 0.05 and look at the left edge.

explain.text: At $p = 0.5$, $np(1-p) = 7.5$ and the bell hugs the bars. At $p = 0.05$ it is only 1.43: the bars lean against 0 and the curve spills below it. A common rule of thumb asks for $np(1-p) \ge 10$.

screens.title: Where should the area start?
screens.prose: A trader wins each of 20 independent trades with chance 0.55, so $X \sim \text{Bin}(20, 0.55)$. We want $P(X \ge 15)$. Bar 15 stands on the stretch from 14.5 to 15.5.
screens.question: To cover bars 15 to 20 with area under the normal curve, where should that area start?

options.why: Starting at 15 cuts bar 15 in half. Its left half, from 14.5 to 15, is missed.
Starting at 15.5 drops bar 15 altogether. You moved the cut the wrong way.
Starting at 14 adds half of bar 14, which is not in $X \ge 15$.

hints.text: Each bar is one unit wide, centred on its whole number.
Bar 15 spans 14.5 to 15.5.
To include all of bar 15, start at its left edge.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the left edge of bar 15.

explain.text: Each whole number $k$ owns the strip from $k - 0.5$ to $k + 0.5$. So $X \ge 15$ is the area from 14.5 up. Moving the cut by half a unit is the **continuity correction**.

screens.title: Put a number on it
screens.question: What is the normal estimate of $P(X \ge 15)$, starting the area at 14.5? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Standardise 14.5: subtract 11, divide by 2.225.
$z = 3.5 / 2.225 \approx 1.573$, and you want the area above it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Standardise 14.5, then take the upper tail.

byKey.phi: That is the area below 14.5. You want the area above it.
byKey.at15: That starts the area at 15, without the correction.
byKey.at155: That starts at 15.5, which drops bar 15.

explain.text: The estimate is 0.0579. Summing the six bars exactly gives 0.0553. Half a unit made the difference between a good estimate and a poor one.

screens.title: Exact against approximate
screens.prose: Compare the three answers for $P(X \ge 15)$. Without the correction the area starts at 15: $z = 4 / 2.225 = 1.798$ and $\Phi(1.798) = 0.9639$.
screens.question: Fill the gaps. Give each error as estimate minus exact, to 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The uncorrected estimate is $1 - 0.9639$.
Subtract 0.0553 from each estimate. A low estimate gives a negative error.

feedback.correct: The correction cuts the error from about 0.019 to about 0.003.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each error is estimate minus 0.0553.

explain.text: Without the correction the estimate is a third too low. With it, the error is under 0.003. The correction costs nothing and fixes most of the gap.

screens.title: Which way does the half go?
screens.prose: Same trader. Now we want $P(X < 9)$, the chance of fewer than 9 wins out of 20.
screens.question: Where should the normal area end?

options.why: You added a half to 9 by habit. But $X < 9$ means $X \le 8$, and bar 8 ends at 8.5.
Ending at 9 takes in half of bar 9, which is not in $X < 9$.
Ending at 7.5 drops bar 8. The correction widens the event to include whole bars.

hints.text: Rewrite $X < 9$ with $\le$ first.
Fewer than 9 means 8 or fewer: the shaded bars.
The last shaded bar is 8. Where is its right edge?

feedback.correct: $X < 9$ is $X \le 8$, whose last bar ends at 8.5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn $X < 9$ into $X \le 8$, then find the edge of bar 8.

byKey.95: You added a half to 9 by habit. But $X < 9$ means $X \le 8$, and bar 8 ends at 8.5.
byKey.75: You subtracted a half from 8. That drops bar 8; the correction must include whole bars.

explain.text: Rewrite the event as whole bars first: $X \le 8$. Then move to the outer edge of the last bar, 8.5. The estimate $\Phi(-1.124) = 0.1306$ sits beside the exact 0.1308.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: You widened each event to whole bars. For $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ with $np(1-p)$ large enough, $$P(X \le k) \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{k + 0.5 - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right).$$ For $P(X \ge k)$, start the area at $k - 0.5$.
screens.question: Which interval of the normal estimates $P(X = 12)$?

options.why: A normal gives any single point probability 0. Bar 12 is a strip one unit wide.
That is only the right half of bar 12.
That takes in half of bars 11 and 13 as well.

hints.text: Bar 12 is one unit wide. Where are its edges?

feedback.correct: Bar 12 is the strip from 11.5 to 12.5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both edges of bar 12.

explain.text: Each value $k$ owns $[k - 0.5, k + 0.5]$. For Bin(20, 0.55), $P(X = 12) \approx \Phi(0.674) - \Phi(0.225) = 0.161$, against an exact 0.162. The rule of thumb $np(1-p) \ge 10$ is cautious; near $p = 0.5$ the fit is good sooner.

screens.title: Why a binomial is nearly normal
screens.prose: Let $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ count successes in $n$ independent trials. Justify the approximation for $P(X \ge k)$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $X = I_1 + \dots + I_n$, where $I_j$ is 1 if trial $j$ succeeds and 0 otherwise
Each $I_j$ has mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)$, and the $I_j$ are independent
By the central limit theorem, $X \approx N\big(np, np(1-p)\big)$ for large $n$
$X$ is a whole number, so $P(X \ge k) = P(X > k - 0.5)$

hints.text: Start by writing $X$ as a sum.
Sum, moments of one trial, the theorem, the half-unit, then standardise.

feedback.correct: A binomial is a sum of indicators, so the theorem applies.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The theorem needs a sum, so write $X$ as one first.

byKey.clt: The theorem needs the sum and the moments of each term first.
byKey.phi: Standardising comes last, after the event is widened to $X > k - 0.5$.

explain.text: The binomial is a sum of $n$ independent 0 or 1 draws, so it inherits the bell. The half-unit step is what makes a smooth curve fit whole-number bars. The lopsided 0 or 1 draws with $p$ near 0 are why small $np(1-p)$ fits badly.

screens.title: When the bell is the wrong tool
screens.prose: $X \sim \text{Bin}(100, 0.02)$, so $np = 2$ and $np(1-p) = 1.96$. For $P(X \ge 5)$: exact 0.0508, Poisson(2) gives 0.0527, normal with the correction gives 0.0371.
screens.question: Which approximation should you use here, and why?

options.text: The Poisson, since $p$ is tiny and the bars lean against 0

options.why: You looked at $n$ alone. What matters is $np(1-p) = 1.96$, far below 10.

options.text: Either, since both are within 0.02 of the exact value
options.why: The normal is 27% too low. In a tail estimate, that is a big miss.

options.text: Neither: only the exact sum will do
options.why: The Poisson is within 0.002 here, and far quicker by hand.

hints.text: Compare each estimate with 0.0508.
Then check $np(1-p)$ against the rule of thumb.

feedback.correct: Rare events in many trials are Poisson territory.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two estimates with the exact 0.0508.

explain.text: With $p$ near 0, the binomial is lopsided, like the Poisson with $\lambda = np$. The Poisson misses by 0.002; the normal by 0.014. For $p$ near 1, count failures instead and use the same idea.

screens.title: Sixty wins from a coin
screens.prose: A strategy's trades are coin flips: each wins with chance 0.5, independently. Over 100 trades, $X \sim \text{Bin}(100, 0.5)$, with mean 50 and sd 5. Use $\Phi(1.9) = 0.9713$.
screens.question: Estimate the chance of at least 60 winning trades, with the continuity correction. Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: At least 60 starts at the left edge of bar 60.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start the area at 59.5 and take the upper tail.

byKey.phi: That is the area below 59.5. Take the upper tail.

explain.text: The estimate is 0.0287 against an exact 0.0284. So a coin-flip strategy hits 60 wins in 100 about one time in 35. A 60% hit rate over 100 trades is suggestive, not proof.

screens.title: Defaults in a loan book
screens.prose: A book holds 1,000 loans, each defaulting with chance 0.02, independently. So $np = 20$ and $np(1-p) = 19.6$. Use $\Phi(2.146) = 0.9841$.
screens.question: What is the quick normal estimate of the chance of 30 or more defaults? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The sd is $\sqrt{19.6} \approx 4.427$.
$z = 9.5 / 4.427 \approx 2.146$; take the upper tail.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at 29.5, divide by $\sqrt{19.6}$, and take the upper tail.

byKey.var: You divided by 19.6, the variance. Use the sd, $\sqrt{19.6} \approx 4.43$.
byKey.phi: That is the area below 29.5. Take the upper tail.

explain.text: The normal says 0.0159; the exact answer is 0.0207, and the Poisson gives 0.0218. Even with $np(1-p) = 19.6$, the right tail is heavier than the bell. Real defaults are also correlated, which fattens that tail further.

ideas: $\text{Bin}(n, p)$ is a sum of $n$ indicators. So it is close to $N(np, np(1-p))$ when $np(1-p)$ is large, 10 as a rule of thumb.
Each value $k$ owns the strip $[k - 0.5, k + 0.5]$: widen the event to whole bars before standardising.
When $p$ is near 0 or 1 the bars are lopsided; the Poisson with $\lambda = np$ does better.

formula.name: Normal approximation with continuity correction
formula.note: For $P(X \ge k)$ start at $k - 0.5$. Rewrite $<$ and $>$ as $\le$ and $\ge$ first.

summary.trap: Adding 0.5 by habit: $P(X < 9)$ is $P(X \le 8)$, which ends at 8.5, not 9.5.

quiz.prose: A poll asks 1,000 random voters a yes or no question. The true share saying yes is 0.5.
quiz.question: Within about how much of 0.5 does the poll's share land, 95% of the time?

options.why: You used the sd of one voter, 0.5, over $\sqrt{10}$. Divide by $\sqrt{1000}$.
You divided by 1,000, not $\sqrt{1000}$.
Each voter is noisy, but the share of 1,000 is not.

feedback.correct: sd of the share $= \sqrt{0.25/1000} \approx 0.0158$, and 2 sds is about 0.03.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the sd of the share, then double it.

explain.text: The count of yes votes is Bin(1000, 0.5), so the share has sd $\sqrt{0.5 \times 0.5 / 1000} \approx 0.0158$. About 95% of polls land within $1.96 \times 0.0158 \approx 0.031$. That is the familiar plus or minus 3 points.

quiz.prose: $X \sim \text{Bin}(100, 0.5)$, with mean 50 and sd 5. You want $P(X \le 40)$ with the continuity correction.
quiz.question: What $z$ value do you look up in $\Phi$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. End the area at the right edge of bar 40.

byKey.nocc: That ends at 40, without the correction.
byKey.wrongway: That ends at 39.5, which drops bar 40.

explain.text: $X \le 40$ ends at 40.5, so $z = -1.9$ and $P \approx \Phi(-1.9) = 0.0287$. The exact value is 0.0284.

quiz.question: Estimate $P(X = 50)$ with the continuity correction. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the area from 49.5 to 50.5.

byKey.zero: A single point has zero area. Use the strip from 49.5 to 50.5.
byKey.half: That is $\Phi(0.1)$, the area below 50.5. Subtract the area below 49.5.

explain.text: The strip from 49.5 to 50.5 is $z = -0.1$ to $0.1$, area $0.0796$. The exact value is 0.0796 too.

quiz.prose: The rule of thumb asks for $np(1-p) \ge 10$ before using the normal.
quiz.question: Which binomial passes it?

options.why: Large $n$, but $np(1-p) \approx 4.98$. Use the Poisson.
$np(1-p) = 2.7$, too small.
$np(1-p) = 1.8$. The bars lean against 20.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $np(1-p)$ for each.

explain.text: Only $\text{Bin}(50, 0.5)$ reaches it: $12.5$. The others have $p$ near 0 or 1, where the bars are lopsided.
